books.section: Topic 4.10 The Second Great Awakening, A. Religious and Spiritual Movements in Antebellum America

stimulus.text: The engraving shows an outdoor religious meeting at Eastham, Massachusetts, in 1852. A preacher stands on a raised wooden platform beside a clapboard building, arm raised, speaking to a large crowd seated on long benches under the trees. Men in top hats and women in bonnets and shawls listen together in the open air. The caption printed beneath the scene reads: "Exhortation and preaching at the camp meeting at Eastham."
stimulus.source_note: Description records only what the engraving visibly shows. Engraving: "Exhortation and preaching at the camp meeting at Eastham," 1852, Library of Congress, LCCN 2003654805. Public domain; image viewed before writing.

source: original; stimulus is a description of a public-domain 1852 engraving (Library of Congress)
stem: Compared with worship in an established eighteenth-century church, the gathering in the engraving most directly shows which change?

options.text: Religion reaching ordinary people outdoors, outside church walls and formal ritual
Religion becoming the exclusive preserve of college-educated ministers and their congregations
options.misconception: The preacher stands above the crowd, so he can look like a scholar speaking to an educated few.

options.text: Religion turning away from emotion toward quiet, orderly study of doctrine
options.misconception: The crowd sits still on benches, which can look like quiet study rather than an emotional meeting.

options.text: Religion withdrawing from public life into small, separate sects
options.misconception: A single meeting in a small town can look like a sect keeping to itself, away from public life.

rationales.A: The crowd sits outdoors on benches under trees, listening to plain preaching. That is religion leaving the building to meet ordinary people where they are.
rationales.B: The listeners are ordinary men and women in work clothes and bonnets, not a college-educated few. The preacher speaks to the crowd, not to scholars.
rationales.C: Camp meetings were emotional by design: exhortation, public conversions, and crowds responding aloud. Quiet doctrinal study is the opposite of what the scene shows.
rationales.D: The meeting is large and public, drawing a crowd together. Withdrawal into small sects would look like the opposite of this open gathering.
rationales.general:
1. Compare the buildings: an eighteenth-century service happened inside a church, under a steeple, led by ritual.
2. Compare the audience: here the audience is a mixed crowd on benches outdoors, not pew-holding members.
3. Compare the preaching: one voice exhorting a crowd, plain and emotional, not a learned sermon.
Background: Revival preachers carried religion to frontier settlements and towns without churches.
Remember: the building tells you who religion was for; the field tells you who it was reaching for.

figures.caption: Exhortation and preaching at the camp meeting at Eastham, Massachusetts, 1852.
figures.alt: An 1852 engraving of a preacher on a raised outdoor platform speaking to a large crowd seated on benches under trees
